name: Mouth breathing correction / myofunctional therapy

lead: Mouth breathing correction is a set of habits and exercises that push breathing through the nose and keep the tongue resting against the palate, sometimes with lip taping at night. People pursue it for a better airway and, they hope, a more defined jaw and better-developed face.

Proponents say tongue posture and nasal airflow shape the jaws and airway. Chronic mouth breathing in children has been proposed to influence dental and facial growth, including a long, narrow face, though the relationship may run in both directions, and that support comes mainly from textbooks, reviews and conceptual models. Myofunctional therapy is studied for breathing and sleep apnea; studies of changing adult facial structure were not found in the sources reviewed.

paras: People practise tongue and lip exercises, hold a nasal-breathing habit during the day and sometimes tape the lips at night. It is often combined with treating nasal congestion, which is the usual cause of mouth breathing. Breathing changes are usually judged over weeks; facial claims play out over much longer.

The health effects of mouth taping have been little researched, according to encyclopedic sources. Persistent mouth breathing can reflect nasal obstruction or other conditions that merit assessment, and taping is generally not advised for people with blocked noses or untreated sleep apnea.

angle.text: Users practise nasal breathing, tongue posture and lip exercises, sometimes taping the lips at night, hoping for a better airway and a more defined jaw and face. Myofunctional therapy has been studied for breathing; the facial-structure link rests mainly on conceptual models.

lead: Mouth breathing correction describes efforts to shift breathing from the mouth to the nose, including exercises of the tongue and lips known as myofunctional therapy and, in some communities, taping the lips shut during sleep. [1]

In about 85% of cases, mouth breathing is described as an adaptation to nasal congestion. [1] Chronic mouth breathing in children has been proposed to influence dental and facial growth, including a long, narrow face, though the relationship may run in both directions. [1]
Support for these links comes mainly from textbooks, reviews and conceptual models, and the health effects of mouth taping are little researched. [1]

paras: About 85% of cases are attributed to nasal congestion, with less common causes including polyps and lip incompetence. [1] Proposed effects include long face syndrome, anterior open bite and tongue thrusting. [1]

The main approach described is treating any underlying nasal obstruction and building a habit of nasal breathing. [1] Myofunctional therapy is mentioned as a related field studied with orthodontics, without evidence of its effectiveness being described. [1]
No studies found in the sources reviewed for this entry. Wikipedia reports that evidence on mouth-breathing and facial growth is largely conceptual or from limited cephalometric work. [1]
